content: Vaginal discharge refers to secretions from the vagina. These secretions can vary in consistency (thick, pasty, thin), color (clear, cloudy, white, yellow, green), and smell (normal, odorless, or foul-smelling). Considerations: It is normal to have some vaginal discharge, especially if you are of childbearing age. The glands in the cervix produce a clear mucus, which may turn white or yellow when exposed to air. These variations are considered normal. The amount of mucus produced by the cervical glands changes throughout the menstrual cycle, depending on the levels of circulating estrogen. Similarly, the vaginal walls also release secretions, and the amount depends on hormone levels in the body. However, if vaginal discharge suddenly changes in color, odor, or consistency, or if there is a significant increase or decrease in the amount, it may indicate an underlying issue such as an infection. Causes of Vaginal Discharge: Normal increases in discharge can occur due to: Emotional stress Ovulation (release of an egg from the ovary mid-cycle) Pregnancy Sexual arousal Abnormal vaginal discharge may result from: Atrophic vaginitis: Common in postmenopausal women with low estrogen levels. Bacterial vaginosis (BV): Overgrowth of bacteria normally present in the vagina, leading to a gray discharge and a fishy odor, which worsens after sexual intercourse. BV is usually not sexually transmitted. Cervical or vaginal cancer: Rarely a cause of excessive discharge. Chlamydia: A sexually transmitted infection. Desquamative vaginitis and lichen planus: Inflammatory conditions. Forgotten tampon or foreign body: Can lead to abnormal discharge. Gonorrhea: A sexually transmitted infection. Other infections and sexually transmitted diseases (STDs). Trichomoniasis: A parasitic infection. Vaginal yeast infection: Caused by an overgrowth of Candida species. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Contact your doctor immediately if: Your discharge is accompanied by fever or pelvic/abdominal pain. You have been exposed to a sexual partner with gonorrhea, chlamydia, or another STD. You experience increased thirst or appetite, unexplained weight loss, increased urinary frequency, or fatigue, as these may be signs of diabetes. A child who has not reached puberty has vaginal discharge. You suspect your discharge is related to a medication. You are concerned about a possible STD or are unsure of potential exposure. Your symptoms worsen or persist for more than one week despite home care. You have blisters or other lesions on your vagina or vulva. You experience burning during urination or other urinary symptoms, which may indicate a urinary tract infection. Diagnosis: Your doctor will take a detailed medical history and perform a physical examination, including a pelvic exam. Questions may include: When did the abnormal discharge begin?
